title: The other handle
hook: everything has two handles; take your brother by "he is my brother," not "he wronged me" (Enchiridion 43)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Socrates, and the idea that nobody does wrong knowingly. Your line was lighter to carry.

A pot on the stove has two handles. One has been sitting over the flame, and it's scorching. The other is cool. Grab the hot one and you drop the pot, and now there's soup on the floor and a burn on your hand. Nobody would blame the pot. You just picked it up by the wrong side. Section forty-three of the Enchiridion is about that choice, and Epictetus aims it straight at family.
screen: `A POT WITH TWO HANDLES.` → `ONE HOT, ONE COOL.` → `THE OTHER HANDLE.`

segments.voice: Everything has two handles, Epictetus says: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can't. The pot is today's picture, not his, but the handles are his. If your brother wrongs you, he says, don't take hold of it by the handle he wronged me. That's the handle by which it can't be carried. Take it by the other one: he's my brother, we were raised together. Then you'll be holding it by the handle that can be carried. The wrong still happened; Epictetus doesn't pretend otherwise. What changes is which fact you pick up first. Grab he wronged me, and every other fact arranges itself around the injury. Grab he's my brother, and the injury becomes one fact inside a longer story, a story with a shared childhood and a kitchen table and probably a few wrongs going the other way. Same situation, different handle, different weight. It works beyond brothers. A coworker, a neighbor, a parent, a friend who let you down. Each relationship has its own cool handle: she's been loyal for ten years. He's my father. We've built this together. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: my own size. Mind the step. The foot measures. Honor the character. Mind first. It seemed right to him. Yesterday and today belong together: first you see why they did it, then you choose how to hold it.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAS TWO HANDLES.` · `NOT 'HE WRONGED ME.' 'HE'S MY BROTHER.'` · `SAME FACTS, DIFFERENT WEIGHT.` · `EVERY RELATIONSHIP HAS A COOL HANDLE.` · then, large: `THE OTHER HANDLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one conflict you're carrying with someone close, and notice which handle you've been holding it by: what they did, what they said, how hot it is. Then gently look for the other handle: who they are to you, what you've shared, what's true about them besides this. Pick the whole thing up by that one fact, and notice the difference in weight.
Two handles, Epictetus says everything has: one that can be carried, and one that can't. Pick up your brother by the one that can. Today's word.
Your line: he's my brother. The cool handle is often the older story. Day three hundred seventy-eight, and another week done.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often reframe a conflict with someone close by starting from the relationship rather than the offense, following Epictetus' image of the two handles.

notes: Enchiridion 43 paraphrased: everything has two handles, one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not; if your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of it by the handle that he wrongs you, but by the other, that he is your brother, nurtured with you.
